q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE difference between Aztec and Inca political organization.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why the Inca Empire was more centralized than the Aztec Empire, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE similarity in how the Aztec and Inca Empires expanded.

sample_answers.a: The Inca built a highly centralized bureaucracy with a state religion, official language (Quechua), and vast road network, while the Aztec ruled through the Triple Alliance — a looser system in which conquered city-states kept their rulers and paid tribute.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, the Inca conquered a long, narrow Andean corridor that they knit together with roads, storehouses, and resettled populations, creating direct administrative control; the Aztec, expanding across Mesoamerica's competing city-states, found it easier to demand tribute than to administer directly.
sample_answers.c: Both empires expanded through military conquest in the fifteenth century, subjugating neighboring peoples and extracting tribute in goods and labor to support their capitals and armies.

q1.stimulus:
Historians compare the Aztec and Inca Empires as the two great indigenous states of the Americas, alike in their rapid fifteenth-century expansion yet different in organization. The Inca created the more centralized system: a divine emperor, a bureaucracy that counted every subject and llama, a 25,000-mile road network, and a policy of resettling conquered peoples to break local loyalties. The Aztec Empire was in practice a tribute system run by the Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan; conquered cities kept their own rulers and gods, provided they delivered regular tribute in maize, cloth, warriors, and sacrificial victims. Both empires were thus extractive — but the Inca extracted through administration, the Aztec through intimidation.
—Historian's account of American empires in the period c. 1200–1450

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE feature of Tenochtitlan that amazed Díaz and his companions.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Díaz's account shows the scale of Aztec civilization.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Díaz compares Tenochtitlan to the enchantments of a romance.

sample_answers.a: Díaz was amazed by the city's great towers, temples, and buildings rising from the water of the lake, with causeways and canals — a metropolis larger and more orderly than anything the Spaniards had seen.
sample_answers.b: His description of many cities and villages, great masonry towers, and dense construction conveys a populous, wealthy, architecturally sophisticated civilization rivaling European capitals.
sample_answers.c: The city's splendor exceeded his expectations so completely that it seemed unreal, like magic; the comparison reveals both genuine wonder and the Spanish tendency to frame the unfamiliar through European literary fantasies.

q2.stimulus:
When we saw so many cities and villages built in the water and other great towns on dry land, we were amazed and said that it was like the enchantments they tell of in the legend of Amadis, on account of the great towers and temples and buildings rising from the water, and all built of masonry. And some of our soldiers even asked whether the things that we saw were not a dream. It is not to be wondered at that I here write it down in this manner, for there is so much to think over that I do not know how to describe it.
—Bernal Díaz del Castillo, The True History of the Conquest of New Spain, c. 1568

q3.directions: Use the map below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern shown on the map of the Aztec Empire in 1519.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the map reflects the Aztec system of tribute.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between the Aztec Empire shown on the map and the Inca Empire at its height.

sample_answers.a: The map shows the Triple Alliance's core (Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, Tlacopan) surrounded by tributary provinces across central Mexico, with strategic provinces on the frontiers — an empire organized as concentric rings of control.
sample_answers.b: The distinction between tributary provinces (which paid regular tribute) and strategic provinces (client states providing aid) shows an empire designed to extract resources rather than to administer territory directly.
sample_answers.c: The Aztec Empire was a compact tribute network in Mesoamerica, while the Inca Empire stretched over 2,500 miles along the Andes with a unified road system and direct bureaucratic administration — far larger and more centralized.

q3.stimulus: The map shows the territorial organization of the Aztec Empire in 1519, on the eve of the Spanish conquest. The Triple Alliance core — Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan — is surrounded by tributary provinces (required to deliver regular tribute in goods and captives) and strategic provinces (allied client states on the frontiers). The map illustrates an empire built on tribute extraction rather than direct administration.
